about.title: About
about.headline: I write frontend that holds up under load
body: Frontend engineer. Four years in production.

What interests me is not the markup but what sits behind it: how the state is arranged, what happens between frames, why a table starts stuttering at five hundred rows and what to do about it. I work in both React and Vue — not "familiar with both", but two production codebases I had to switch between mid-week.

Over those years a set of problems piled up that were interesting to solve and are worth talking about. The most telling ones I have rebuilt here from scratch: every claim that carries a number becomes its own demo — you can run it right on the page and watch the counter.

principles.title: Measure first, then write
principles.body: Optimising without measuring is guessing. Twice while building these demos the measurement showed that the "slow" version was in fact the faster one, and it was the demo that had to be rewritten, not the wording.

principles.title: Boundaries over polish
principles.body: FSD, public APIs per slice, a linter that catches an import going upwards. Fifty modules and three teams in one repository live on hard boundaries — not on agreements.

principles.title: Tests where mistakes are expensive
principles.body: Not for a coverage number. A buffer collapse that quietly changes data is caught only by a property check over generated sessions; a panel printing the wrong schema, only by a test that checks it against the validator.

footer.builtWith: Built with Next.js, GSAP and a strict grid.

demos.vueNote: This demo is real Vue 3 running inside a React page. The Vue code sits in a separate file and does not load with the page: the browser fetches it later, and the demo starts once you have scrolled down to it.
demos.reactNote: This demo is React, same as the original project. Its code sits in a separate file too, does not load with the page, and starts once you have scrolled down to it.
demos.portNote: This demo is React; in the project it was Vue 3. What matters here is the mechanism, not the framework. The code sits in a separate file too and starts once you have scrolled down to it.

undoRedo.title: Undo buffer
undoRedo.lead: Drag the blocks, add one, delete one, rename one. Every action goes into one shared list. Before anything is sent to the server that list is squeezed: what travels is the result of your work, not every twitch of the mouse.
undoRedo.connecting: Now pick the second block — the link appears, or goes away.
undoRedo.hint: Drag a block, or tap one to select it. A whole drag counts as one action — ⌘Z undoes the entire gesture, not its last millimetre.
undoRedo.coverage: Six action types here, over forty in the real editor. The mechanism does not care how many there are.

canvasFps.title: The frame budget
canvasFps.lead: The same picture and the same animation, drawn on screen two different ways. Flip the mode and watch the frame counter: the difference is not your machine, it is how much extra work the code does between frames.
canvasFps.canvas: A field of blocks and links
canvasFps.reads: Questions to the browser per frame
canvasFps.hint: The modes are measured one at a time: the browser paints on a single thread, and two scenes side by side would fight over it. The first thirty frames after a switch do not count — they are warm-up. Hit pause and compare the “loop” line.
canvasFps.naiveNote: The naive mode moves blocks with the left/top properties, which make the browser recompute the page layout. Worse, the code alternates: it asks the browser where a block is now, then immediately moves it. Every question asked right after a move forces the browser to redo the layout on the spot, mid-frame, dozens of times in a row. The frame misses its 16 millisecond budget and the picture stutters.
canvasFps.budgetNote: Exactly the same work: every block and every link is repositioned, with no cleverness about updating only what changed. Two things differ. The code takes coordinates from its own memory instead of asking the browser, so nothing forces a layout mid-frame. And it moves blocks with transform, which the browser hands to the graphics card without touching layout. While paused, no frame is drawn at all.

txTable.title: A table under live data
txTable.lead: Five hundred transactions, with statuses changing every second as if a server were pushing them. The highlight is not decoration: a row lights up at the exact moment the browser repainted it. Turn either checkbox off and watch how many rows light up instead of one.
txTable.hint: The data is made up: merchant names are generated, amounts are random. What the NDA covers is the client's code, not how a table is rendered.
txTable.note: Virtualisation means drawing only what fits in the window: a couple of dozen rows live in the page instead of five hundred, so scrolling no longer slows down as the list grows. Memoisation solves the other half: when one status changes, one row is repainted rather than the whole table. It only works because the untouched rows stay the very same objects in memory. Copy the whole list on every message and memoisation saves nothing.

dynamicForm.title: A form that knows its own rules
dynamicForm.lead: Switch the payout method and it is not just the fields that change — the validation rules change too. They are printed in full on the right: not an illustration, but the actual code that is checking the form right now.
dynamicForm.hint: The rules follow more than the method: for a crypto payout the address is checked against the network you picked — change it and watch the address pattern change. Values the new rules have no place for are dropped: an IBAN must not travel to the server alongside a card payout.
dynamicForm.note: The rules are written once, as a single list. Both the validation itself and the text beside the form are built from that list, so there is nowhere for them to drift apart. A test holds it: the panel must show every rule the form actually checks against.

liveRollup.title: Numbers that survive a change of scale
liveRollup.lead: One stream of events and two ways of computing the same number from it. The first recounts every event from scratch — honest and expensive. The second adds up ready-made five-second totals — cheap, and what almost every dashboard does. Switch the scale (5 seconds, a minute, 5 minutes) and watch which numbers stay identical and which quietly drift apart.
liveRollup.chart: Two ways of counting one stream, over the same window
liveRollup.hint: Turn on the gap in the stream: the honest count leaves a hole in the chart, the cheap one draws a zero. But a zero and “we measured nothing” are different things. That is exactly the lie a food tracker tells when it prints 0 mg for a nutrient nobody ever measured.
liveRollup.note: Sums and counts can be added up: a minute is the sum of its twelve five-second pieces, and no regrouping changes the answer. Averages already cannot: to combine two averages you need to know how many events stand behind each, and those counts are gone once the totals are stored. p95 cannot be combined at all. p95 is the line below which 95% of the values fall — to find it you need the values themselves, not somebody else's totals. No formula turns twelve stored p95 values into the p95 of the minute. So the dashed line on the chart is not an approximate answer. It is a confident answer to a different question.

foodMatch.title: The row you pick is the answer
foodMatch.lead: Type a food. The same rows from the USDA reference, sorted two ways: the obvious one — shortest name, most measurements — and the one the product actually ships. The calories at the top differ by a factor of three, and the panel on the right shows which rule the two answers parted on.
foodMatch.substring: match the name as a fragment
foodMatch.nothing: No food by that name in this slice of the reference.

rules.standIn: imitations and baby food go last
rules.unqualified: a plain name, with no qualifiers, wins
rules.dataset: the source closer to everyday speech
rules.processing: the right form: raw or cooked
rules.aspect: “part not specified” means the whole food
rules.id: row id, so the order never wobbles

foodMatch.hint: “Buckwheat” is 343 kcal; “Buckwheat groats” is 118. Neither name is wrong, and the reference cannot tell you which one a person meant. Only the kind of food can: buckwheat is eaten cooked, an apple is eaten raw. So the code doing the asking states “this food is eaten cooked”, and the sorting takes that into account. Turn the same flag on for an apple and watch the answer get worse.
foodMatch.note: There is no model here: the row is picked by an ordinary sort over eight rules in sequence. If two rows tie on the first rule, the second decides, then the third, and so on. That is deliberate: picking the row means picking the calories and the protein, so the decision has to come out the same every time and be explainable by a list of rules. The rules read the name in whole chunks between commas rather than as separate words: “Cheese, Parmesan, dry grated” is grated parmesan, while a search for the word “dry” calls it dry cheese. The code here is the same code that runs in production. Only the reference is cut down — 154 rows across 18 foods — so every candidate being sorted fits on screen.

guardrails.title: What holds a rule up
guardrails.lead: Eight edits an AI agent might propose on the FoodIQ frontend, and three levels of checking that meet them. A level does not answer whether the edit is bad; it answers what finding out costs. The build answers for free and always the same way. A meter names a number. A chain of four AI reviewers thinks — and every answer it gives costs money.

gateNames.contract: request code against the API spec

meterNames.specs: modules with logic but no tests

guardrails.notReached: Not run: the edit was stopped at an earlier level.

outcomes.build: The edit does not go in, and no reviewer decided that: the project simply does not build with it.
outcomes.threshold: The number is over the limit, and the edit does not go in. A limit is not truth, it is a budget: it stands so that the increase gets noticed the day it is made.
outcomes.chain: The automated checks are silent; an AI reviewer objects. It cannot reject the edit — only name a price somebody would otherwise pay without looking.

guardrails.passed: All three levels are silent, and the edit goes in. A check that never lets anything through is not a check, it is a wall.

guardrails.hint: The objections appear exactly as the reviewers wrote them, in the language they read this codebase in — a Russian objection does not turn English because you opened the site in English.
guardrails.note: An instruction for an agent is only advice. On the FoodIQ frontend it runs to 129 KB and 3,360 lines across fourteen files, and no model holds that in its head on every edit. So the question is not whether to write rules, it is where to put each one. The costliest example is right here: the rules about which code may use which were written out in full and were not running at all, because they sat in an old-format config that the current linter no longer reads. A written rule and a running rule are different things, and the difference surfaces on exactly the day somebody goes looking. Whatever a machine can decide goes down into the build and stops being prose: porting the config surfaced 358 violations, and today there are 30. Whatever can be measured becomes a number somebody watches. Everything else goes to the AI reviewers, and that is where checking starts costing money. There are four reviewers rather than one because a single reviewer holding every rule at once approves everything. The build has its own blind spot too: it does not see code pulled in on the fly, so only a reviewer catches that edit. The demo runs the rules, not the tooling: there is no linter and no test runner in your browser, and the file tree is a fixture. What is real is the rules, the numbers and the objections — they came out of an actual run of the agents on that project.

accessMatrix.title: Permissions live in one place
accessMatrix.lead: Four roles over one queue of tickets. Every access rule lives in a single module: the interface knows none of them and only asks the question — may this person do this to this ticket? The answer depends not on the role in general but on the particular row: whose flat it is, who it is assigned to, whether the work is done. Switch to the familiar “just check the role inside the button” and it agrees with the rules right up to the first ticket belonging to somebody else.

rules.operatorRead: An operator reads every ticket in the queue.
rules.operatorAssign: An operator assigns a ticket while it is still new.
rules.dispatcherRead: A dispatcher reads every ticket in the queue.
rules.dispatcherAssign: A dispatcher assigns any ticket, at any point.
rules.dispatcherClose: A dispatcher closes a ticket that is assigned to them.
rules.accountantRead: An accountant reads every ticket in the queue.
rules.accountantInvoice: An accountant invoices a ticket once the work is done.
rules.residentRead: A resident reads tickets from their own flat.
rules.residentClose: A resident confirms work done in their own flat.

accessMatrix.ask: Press an action on a row — that is the interface asking whether it is allowed.
accessMatrix.noRule: No rule grants it, and that is the whole answer. Nothing was forbidden here specifically — everything is denied by default until a rule allows it.
accessMatrix.diverges: answers the role check gets wrong
accessMatrix.hint: A dispatcher and a resident may both close a ticket — the role says so, and the role is right. Which ticket is a different question, and only the row itself can answer it.
accessMatrix.note: Every rule sits in one file: nine short lines, one branch per role. It is the only place in the project that says who may do what. The interface only asks “is this allowed” and knows nothing about how the answer is produced: a new role means one more branch here, not a hunt for checks scattered across buttons. The rules are written as statements rather than as conditionals sprinkled through the code, so the same list is both applied and shown to the person in the panel on the right. Everything is denied by default: if no rule allowed it, the answer is no. The panel does not match explanations to verdicts by hand — it asks the permissions library (CASL) which rule matched, so the explanation cannot drift away from the decision. The role check beside it is deliberately given no ticket to look at: that is the defect on show. The gap between the two checks is pinned by a test, because a divergence nobody counted is not evidence.

walletState.title: The state around the wallet
walletState.lead: The left panel is a crypto wallet, and you are holding it: approve, refuse, answer that a request is already open, move the network under a running app. The right panel is the application answering. No extension is needed and no real wallet is connected — what is on show is the states the application keeps inside and what it tells a person in each of them.

advice.idle: Nothing has been asked of the wallet yet.
advice.connecting: The request is open in the wallet. There will be no second window — this one is waiting for you, possibly behind the browser.
advice.wrongChain: The wallet is on a network this application does not work in. The connection is intact; the network is not.
advice.switching: The wallet is being asked to switch networks. It can refuse, and refusing changes nothing that already works.
advice.ready: Connected, on the right network, and nothing is pending.
advice.signing: The signature request is open in the wallet.
advice.rejected: The wallet refused. Nothing was sent and nothing was spent — you can ask again.
advice.pending: A request of this kind is already open. Asking again opens nothing: the answer is in the window that is already there.
advice.signed: Signed. The signature is in the application and the connection stayed where it was.

walletState.quiet: The wallet is also allowed to say nothing at all: leave a request unanswered and the application stays in its waiting state rather than deciding on your behalf.
walletState.hint: Refuse a signature and watch what does not happen: the connection stays, the network stays, and the application returns to the state it was in before it asked.
walletState.note: The project used ethers.js here, but the interesting part is not the library — it is the state around it. Six states and one transition table: if a state has no answer for an event, that event does not exist for it, so there is nothing to corrupt. Buttons on both panels are enabled straight from that table rather than from a second list of “what can be clicked now”, which is why the interface cannot drift out of step with the logic. The error codes are real ones: 4001 means the person refused, -32002 means a request window is already open. And the same refusal deliberately reads differently depending on where it lands: refusing while connecting sends you back to the start, refusing while signing costs you nothing.

referralSplit.title: Twelve people and one cent
referralSplit.lead: A referral bonus split across a team in proportion to what each member turned over. Drag the slider: the payouts add up to the bonus at every position. Beside it is the same calculation with each row rounded on its own and nobody adding the column up.
referralSplit.drift: cents the row-by-row rounding is off by
referralSplit.exact: The first number is the whole bonus, to the cent, at every position of the slider. The second is not money anyone lost — it is money nobody reconciled.
referralSplit.hint: A cent is not small change or a rounding error here: it is either paid to somebody or it is not, and both answers have to be the same number.
referralSplit.note: Everything is counted in whole cents, because keeping money in fractional numbers is agreeing to be wrong later. Each share is cut down to a whole cent, and the cents left over go to whoever lost the most in the cut. One sort, and the payouts add up to the bonus whatever its size. Equal leftovers are settled by a fixed order, otherwise the same team would be paid differently depending on how the sort happened to fall today. The tree is not decoration: every branch total equals the sum of what sits under it, and a test checks that against the real payouts rather than against another total computed the same way.
